opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to take some of that pressure off. A lot of people hear "you need to be using AI" and imagine they have to reinvent how they work overnight, and that's just not how it tends to go in practice. The best adoption I've seen starts really small, with one annoying, concrete task.

So for something like Codex, I'd want the product to meet people where they already are. Instead of asking "what could AI do for you?", which is kind of a paralyzing question, it should show up inside the work you're already doing and offer to take something off your plate. Maybe that's writing the tests you've been putting off, tracking down why a build is failing, or explaining an unfamiliar part of the codebase before you touch it. Those are low-stakes, easy to verify, and you get a feel for what the tool is good at.

I also think it matters a lot that people stay in control and can see what's happening. If you hand off a task and get back a giant diff with no explanation, that doesn't build confidence. If you can see the reasoning, review the changes, and push back, you start to calibrate. You learn, "okay, I trust it for this kind of thing, but I want to look closely at that kind of thing." That calibration is really what "knowing where it fits" means.

And honestly, part of it is just giving people permission to experiment without it being a big deal. Try delegating something you'd normally do yourself, see what comes back, and if it's not useful, that's fine, you learned something. Over time the workflow kind of reveals itself. You notice you've stopped doing certain chores by hand, and you're spending more time on the parts of the job you actually care about. That's the outcome we want, not adoption for its own sake.

r001.rationale: The response recommends offering help with concrete tasks inside existing work, but does not say Codex should infer the needed AI workflow from a user's description of their goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because the pressure is real. A lot of people hear "everyone's using AI" and feel this low-grade anxiety that they're falling behind, but when they actually sit down with a tool, they don't know what to hand it. And I'd argue that's not their fault. It's a product failure if the tool requires you to already know how to use it well.

So the first thing I'd say is that the product has to meet you where you are, not where some demo video is. If you're an engineer who's been working a certain way for ten years, you shouldn't have to blow up your workflow to get value. Codex, ideally, should be something you can try on one small, annoying thing. The test you keep meaning to write. The migration you've been avoiding. The bug that's been sitting in the backlog for three weeks. Low stakes, real task, and you see what happens.

The second piece is that the product should help you build intuition, not just produce output. Early on, the most important thing isn't that the model does the task perfectly. It's that you walk away with a clearer sense of what it's good at and where you still need to be the one driving. If someone tries it once, gets a mediocre result on something hard, and concludes "this isn't for me," that's the worst outcome. So we want the first experiences to be ones where you can actually see the shape of the collaboration.

And honestly, I think we should be more upfront about the fact that there isn't one right way to fit this in. Some people want it running in the background on a big refactor while they focus on something else. Some people want it as a pair programmer, going back and forth. Some people just want it to review their work before they open a PR. All of those are legitimate. The product should make it easy to find your version rather than implying there's a correct way everyone else has already figured out.

The last thing I'd say is that the pressure shouldn't come from the tool. It should feel like an option that's there when you want it, and gets out of your way when you don't. If people feel like they're being pushed, they'll resist, and reasonably so. If they feel like it genuinely took something off their plate, they'll come back on their own. That's the bar we should hold ourselves to.

r001.rationale: The response suggests trying small tasks and finding a personal way to use Codex, but does not propose that Codex determine a workflow from the user's description of their goal.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point should be something you already want to get done. If you feel pressure to use AI, being handed a blank box and told, “Ask it anything,” can actually create more work. Now you have to figure out what it’s good at and how to explain your problem.

For something like Codex, I’d want us to make that first useful step easier. Maybe there’s a piece of code you don’t understand, a bug you’ve been putting off, or a repetitive task that takes up part of your day. Start there, with something small enough that you can judge whether the help was useful.

And the product should make it easy to review what happened and stay in control. You build confidence through those experiences. The goal shouldn’t be to make people feel like they’re keeping up with AI. It should be to help them do something they care about, with less friction.

r001.rationale: The response suggests starting with a task the user wants to complete, but does not say Codex should determine the needed AI workflow from the user's description.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to take some of that pressure off. You shouldn’t have to figure out an entirely new way of working just because there’s a new tool. The product should help you find a starting point in something you already do.

So, where do you get stuck? What’s repetitive? What’s something you keep putting off? With Codex, that might be understanding an unfamiliar piece of code or investigating a bug. Start with one concrete task, see what it does, and decide whether that was useful.

And the product has to make that easy to judge. What did it change? Why? How can I check it? That gives people a way to build confidence through experience. The goal shouldn’t be to make people feel like they’re using enough AI. It should be to help them get something done.

r001.rationale: The response suggests starting with a concrete task the user already does and evaluating whether Codex helps. It does not say Codex should determine the needed AI workflow from the user’s description of their goal.
